## Data

This work includes data for all nondemocracies, defined as a Regimes of the World with ambiguous cases (v2x_regime_amb) < 4, Electoral autocracies and below^[Coppedge, Michael, John Gerring, Carl Henrik Knutsen, Staffan I. Lindberg, Jan Teorell, Nazifa Alizada, David Altman, Michael Bernhard, Agnes Cornell, M. Steven Fish, Lisa Gastaldi, Haakon Gjerløw, Adam Glynn, Sandra Grahn, Allen Hicken, Garry Hindle, Nina Ilchenko, Katrin Kinzelbach, Joshua Krusell, Kyle L. Marquardt, Kelly McMann, Valeriya Mechkova, Juraj Medzihorsky, Pamela Paxton, Daniel Pemstein, Josefine Pernes, Oskar Ryden, Johannes von Romer, Brigitte Seim, Rachel Sigman, Svend-Erik Skaaning, Jeffrey Staton, Aksel Sundstrom, Eitan Tzelgov, Yi-ting Wang, Tore Wig, Steven Wilson and Daniel Ziblatt. 2022. "V-Dem [Country-Year/Country-Date] Dataset v12" Varieties of Democracy (V-Dem) Project. https://doi.org/10.23696/vdemds22]. 

## Data Load

```{r echo=FALSE}
options(scipen = 999)
# library(stargazer)
library(here)

autocracies_data <- read.csv(here("data","autocracies_data_v.csv"))

autocracies_data$NAGs_Supported <- autocracies_data$NumNAG_S
autocracies_data$NAGS_with_Training_Camps <- autocracies_data$Num_S_TrainCamp
autocracies_data$Opposition_Size <- autocracies_data$oppsize_norm
autocracies_data$Minimal_Winning_Coalition <- autocracies_data$W_norm
autocracies_data$Distance_Between_Capitals <- autocracies_data$capdist
autocracies_data$Democratizing_Civil_Society_Movement <- autocracies_data$v2csanmvch_4


hurdle_count_n <- autocracies_data[which(autocracies_data$NumNAG_S > 0),]

hurdle_count_t <- autocracies_data[which(autocracies_data$Num_S_TrainCamp >0),]

autocracies_data$at_least_1_NAG_supported <- ifelse(autocracies_data$NAGs_Supported > 0,1,0)

autocracies_data$at_least_1_Training_Camp <- ifelse(autocracies_data$NAGS_with_Training_Camps>0,1,0)

autocracies_data$Training_Camp_and_Democratic_Target <- ifelse((autocracies_data$NAGS_with_Training_Camps>0 & autocracies_data$targ_democratic == 1),1,0)



```

## Models

### Minimal Winning Coalitions and Ideology - prior concepts

I start with some test code examining the effect of minimal winning coalitions^[Bueno de Mesquita, Bruce, and Alastair Smith. “A New Indicator of Coalition Size: Tests against Standard Regime‐type Indicators.” Social Science Quarterly, March 25, 2022. https://doi.org/10.1111/ssqu.13123] and regime ideology^[The main explanatory variable in my previous work.] Smaller W predicts greater use of private payoffs to maintain W. I argued that ideological payoffs substitute for private payoffs.

- HW: Autocratic regimes which have smaller winning coalitions (W)  and are also more reliant on ideological support groups will be more likely to support NAGS, all else equal. 




```{r echo=FALSE}
library(MASS)
library(pscl)
library(VGAM)


formulaw1 <- NAGs_Supported ~ W *  v2exl_legitideol + WarOnTerror + ColdWar + distance_between_capitals  

formulaw1b <- NAGS_with_Training_Camps ~ W * v2exl_legitideol +  WarOnTerror + ColdWar + distance_between_capitals  


# quasipoisson model using number of groups supported

w1_numSq <- glm(formula = formulaw1, family  = quasipoisson(link = "log"), data = autocracies_data)
summary(w1_numSq)
exp(coef(w1_numSq))


# Hurdle model

w1_hurdle <- hurdle(formula = formulaw1, data = autocracies_data)
summary(w1_hurdle)

w1_hurdle_part <- glm(at_least_1_NAG_supported ~ W * v2exl_legitideol +  WarOnTerror + ColdWar + distance_between_capitals , family  = binomial(link = "logit"), data = autocracies_data)
summary(w1_hurdle_part)
exp(coef(w1_hurdle_part))



w1_count_part <- vglm(formula = formulaw1, family  = pospoisson(), data = hurdle_count_n)
summary(w1_count_part)

exp(coef(w1_numSqb))


# Hurdle model

w1_hurdle_partb <- glm(at_least_1_NAG_supported ~ W * v2exl_legitideol + WarOnTerror + ColdWar + distance_between_capitals , family  = binomial(link = "logit"), data = autocracies_data)
```

## Next steps: Instrumental variable using 2SLS Regression with a linear probability model

An obvious concern is that supporting non-state armed groups, especially those targeting democracies, may create an incentive for international actors to support regime change in the state. Specifically, the United States and European democracies have active programs of democracy promotion, which may include both overt support for opposition and efforts that indirectly encourage opposition in the state. To account for this, I use an instrumental variable approach to isolate the exogenous effect of opposition size on support for Non-state Armed Groups. 


### Instrument is Civil Society Organization Women's Participation (v2csgender)

While there is a strong theoretical link between the strength of civil society and the strength of opposition groups, which makes some measure of civil society an appropriate instrument it is necessary to find an appropriate measure of civil society. There are two issues here. First, many measures of civil society include an often heavy emphasis on the sorts of non-governmental organizations that are often the target or even creation of democracy promotion efforts by the West. Thus, these measures suffer the same endogeneity problem the instrumental variable treatment approach is intended to solve. Second, many measures focusing on civil society organizations are one step removed from measuring the strength of civil society especially as related to opposition and instead measure the institutional characteristics of the regime. Developing a separate measure of civil society strength would be worthwhile but well beyond the scope of the current analysis. The VDem data set used here offers several measures which suffer the issues mentioned, but also offers one measure which closely ties civil society to opposition strength both theoretically and empirically  -  women's participation in civil society.

It has been asserted that women's participation in civil society anti-system movements represent a tipping point to large scale opposition, mass protest, and even outright rebellion.^[Henshaw, Alexis Leanna. “Where Women Rebel.” International Feminist Journal of Politics 18, no. 1 (January 2, 2016): 39–60. https://doi.org/10.1080/14616742.2015.1007729] This is seen particularly in the "Woman, Life, Freedom" slogan of the Iranian uprising of 2021-2022.^[Dabiri, Arastoo. “‘Woman, Life, Freedom’: A Movement in Progress in Iran.” Dignity: A Journal of Analysis of Exploitation and Violence 8, no. 1 (2023): 5. https://doi.org/10.23860/dignity.2023.08.01.05]^[Ms Constitution. “‘Woman, Life, Liberty’ in Iran and the Role of Academia.” Nature Human Behaviour 7, no. 1 (January 2023): 3–5. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-022-01504-6]


### Linear Probability Model instead of Generalized Linear Model

For purposes of instrumental variable analysis, I use Two Stage Least Squares, offering a Linear Probability Model of the binary dependent variables.^[“Even with these problems, the linear probability model is useful and often applied in economics. It usually works well for values of the independent variables that are near the averages in the
sample.” (p.209, Wooldridge, Jeffrey. Introductory Econometrics: A Modern Approach. 6th ed. Mason, OH: CENGAGE Learning Custom Publishing, 2015.] 


```{r}


cor(autocracies_data$opposition_size,autocracies_data$v2csgender, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")



cor(autocracies_data$opposition_size,autocracies_data$v2csantimv, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")

library("modelsummary")
library(ivreg)

#Hypothesis H1 as Linear Probability Model

h1_lpm <- lm(at_least_1_NAG_supported ~ opposition_size + WarOnTerror + ColdWar + distance_between_capitals+ W, data = autocracies_data)
summary(h1_lpm)

#H1 as Instrumental Variable 2sLS model

h1_iv <- ivreg(at_least_1_NAG_supported ~ WarOnTerror + ColdWar + distance_between_capitals + W | opposition_size | v2csgender, data = autocracies_data)

summary(h1_iv)

m_list1 <- list(OLS = h1_lpm, IV = h1_iv)
msummary(m_list1)

modelplot(m_list1)

#H2 as Linear Probability Model

h2_lpm <- lm(at_least_1_Training_Camp ~ opposition_size + WarOnTerror + ColdWar + distance_between_capitals  + W + NAGs_Supported, data = autocracies_data)
summary(h2_lpm)

h2i_lpm <- lm(at_least_1_Training_Camp ~ opposition_size + v2exl_legitideolcr_4 + WarOnTerror + ColdWar + distance_between_capitals  + W + NAGs_Supported, data = autocracies_data)
summary(h2i_lpm)

#H2 as 2SLS Instrumental Variable Model

h2_iv <- ivreg(at_least_1_Training_Camp ~ WarOnTerror + ColdWar + distance_between_capitals + W + NAGs_Supported | opposition_size |v2csgender, family  = binomial(link = "logit"), data = autocracies_data)
summary(h2_iv)

h2i_iv <- ivreg(at_least_1_Training_Camp ~ v2exl_legitideolcr_4 + WarOnTerror + ColdWar + distance_between_capitals + W  + NAGs_Supported | opposition_size |v2csgender, family  = binomial(link = "logit"), data = autocracies_data)
summary(h2_iv)

m_list2 <- list(OLS = h2_lpm, IV = h2_iv)
msummary(m_list2)

modelplot(m_list2)

m_list2i <- list(OLS = h2i_lpm, IV = h2i_iv)
msummary(m_list2i)

modelplot(m_list2i)

#h3as LPM

h3_lpm <- lm(Training_Camp_and_Democratic_Target ~ opposition_size + WarOnTerror + ColdWar + distance_between_capitals + W + NAGS_with_Training_Camps, data = autocracies_data)
summary(h3_lpm)

#H3 as 2SLS IV Regression

h3_iv <- ivreg(Training_Camp_and_Democratic_Target ~  WarOnTerror + ColdWar + distance_between_capitals + W + NAGS_with_Training_Camps| opposition_size | v2csgender, data = autocracies_data)

summary(h3_iv)


m_list3 <- list(OLS = h3_lpm, IV = h3_iv)
msummary(m_list3)

modelplot(m_list3)



```
